content.summary: This chapter explores the public API and adapter interfaces of requests, focusing on sessions, transport adapters, cookie jars, and request preparation.

blocks.text: Public API and Adapters

Building upon the overview provided in the previous chapter on the requests library, this chapter examines the public-facing components that handle communication, connection pooling, and request preparation.
Core Session and Adapter Classes

The public interface relies heavily on the Session class, which provides cookie persistence, connection-pooling, and configuration across requests [E2]. The Session class inherits from SessionRedirectMixin [E3] to manage redirect logic.

blocks.code:
class Session(SessionRedirectMixin):
    """A Requests session.

    Provides cookie persistence, connection-pooling, and configuration.

    Basic Usage::

      >>> import requests
      >>> s = requests.Session()
      >>> s.get('https://httpbin.org/get')
      <Response [200]>

    Or as a context manager::

      >>> with requests.Session() as s:
      ...     s.get('https://httpbin.org/get')
      <Response [200]>
    """
blocks.caption: Session class definition

blocks.text: To communicate with HTTP and HTTPS URLs, Requests uses the HTTPAdapter class [E1]. It implements the transport adapter interface for urllib3, managing connection pools and retries [E1].

blocks.code:
class HTTPAdapter(BaseAdapter):
    """The built-in HTTP Adapter for urllib3.

    Provides a general-case interface for Requests sessions to contact HTTP and
    HTTPS urls by implementing the Transport Adapter interface. This class will
    usually be created by the :class:`Session <Session>` class under the
    covers.

    :param pool_connections: The number of urllib3 connection pools to cache.
    :param pool_maxsize: The maximum number of connections to save in the pool.
    :param max_retries: The maximum number of retries each connection
        should attempt. Note, this applies only to failed DNS lookups, socket
        connections and connection timeouts, never to requests where data has
        made it to the server. By default, Requests does not retry failed
        connections. If you need granular control over the conditions under
        which we retry a request, import urllib3's ``Retry`` class and pass
        that instead.
    :param pool_block: Whether the connection pool should block for connections.

    Usage::

      >>> import requests
      >>> s = requests.Session()
      >>> a = requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter(max_retries=3)
      >>> s.mount('http://', a)
    """
blocks.caption: HTTPAdapter class definition

blocks.text: Cookies and Request Preparation

The cookie subsystem supports the public interface through classes such as RequestsCookieJar and MockRequest [E5, E6]. RequestsCookieJar is a compatibility class that inherits from http.cookiejar.CookieJar and MutableMapping to expose a dictionary interface [E5]. MockRequest wraps a requests.Request to mimic a urllib2.Request so that http.cookiejar.CookieJar can correctly manage cookie policies [E6].
When a request is made through a session, prepare_request is called to construct a PreparedRequest for transmission [E7].

content.summary: This chapter explores the internal data structures, compatibility modules, and exception handling mechanisms of the requests library.

blocks.text: Internal Structures and Exceptions

Building upon Overview of Requests Library, this chapter delves deeper into how requests handles data structures, character detection compatibility, and exceptions. Public API and Adapters covers the public HTTP interfaces.
Compatibility and Character Detection
The library includes compatibility modules to resolve character detection libraries dynamically [E1]. The _resolve_char_detection function attempts to import chardet or charset_normalizer [E1].

blocks.caption: Character detection resolution

blocks.text: Case-Insensitive Structures and Status Codes

Responses and prepared requests utilize a CaseInsensitiveDict for headers, which implements MutableMapping so that querying and contains testing are case-insensitive while preserving the case of the last set key [E6, E5, E9].

blocks.code:
class CaseInsensitiveDict(MutableMapping):
    """A case-insensitive ``dict``-like object.

    Implements all methods and operations of
    ``MutableMapping`` as well as dict's ``copy``. Also
    provides ``lower_items``.

    All keys are expected to be strings. The structure remembers the
    case of the last key to be set, and ``iter(instance)``,
    ``keys()``, ``items()``, ``iterkeys()``, and ``iteritems()``
    will contain case-sensitive keys. However, querying and contains
    testing is case insensitive::

        cid = CaseInsensitiveDict()
        cid['Accept'] = 'application/json'
        cid['aCCEPT'] == 'application/json'  # True
        list(cid) == ['Accept']  # True

    For example, ``headers['content-encoding']`` will return the
    value of a ``'Content-Encoding'`` response header, regardless
    of how the header name was originally stored.

    If the constructor, ``.update``, or equality comparison
    operations are given keys that have equal ``.lower()``s, the
    behavior is undefined.
    """
blocks.caption: CaseInsensitiveDict definition

blocks.text: Error Handling and Exceptions

Requests defines a hierarchy of exceptions rooted at RequestException, which inherits from IOError [E2, E7]. All exceptions explicitly raised by Requests inherit from RequestException [E7], with specific error classes including InvalidJSONError and RetryError [E3, E8].

blocks.code:
class RequestException(IOError):
    """There was an ambiguous exception that occurred while handling your
    request.
    """
blocks.caption: RequestException base class

content.summary: This chapter details the configuration files and documentation build processes for the requests repository.

blocks.text: Configuration and Documentation

This chapter builds upon the Overview of Requests Library chapter to explain how the project documentation and repository configurations are structured. Other chapters cover topics like Public API and Adapters and Internal Structures and Exceptions.
Documentation Build Process

The documentation build process is controlled by configuration files such as .readthedocs.yaml and docs/conf.py [E2, E3]. ReadTheDocs uses Ubuntu 22.04 with Python 3.12 to build the documentation [E2]. Sphinx uses extensions like autodoc, intersphinx, todo, and viewcode [E3].
Additionally, docs/make.bat provides Windows command file support for generating Sphinx documentation targets like html, singlehtml, and linkcheck [E4].
Manifest Packaging
Packaging and source distribution files are declared in MANIFEST.in, which includes README.md, LICENSE, NOTICE, HISTORY.md, requirements-dev.txt, tests, and test certificates [E1].

blocks.code:
include README.md LICENSE NOTICE HISTORY.md requirements-dev.txt
recursive-include tests *.py
recursive-include tests/certs *
blocks.caption: Manifest inclusion rules

blocks.text: The documentation configuration in docs/conf.py sets the pygments style to flask_theme_support.FlaskyStyle [E5] and defines epub output options such as epub_exclude_files [E7], while documentation themes include a license detailing modifications by Kenneth Reitz and original work by Armin Ronacher [E8].
